summary: WebinarTV used publicly discoverable Zoom registration or joining links to access sessions and publish recordings, summaries and some AI-hosted podcast versions without organisers’ or participants’ permission in documented cases. In March 2026, 404 Media examined an educators’ session on protecting students from ICE raids that was posted and made into a “Phil & Amy” AI podcast; WebinarTV removed it after the teacher objected. An April investigation found 12-step recovery and patient/caregiver support sessions on the site, including participants’ names and faces and a vetted Graves’ disease family meeting intended not to be recorded. WebinarTV’s chief executive disputed a privacy violation, describing webinars as public and claiming host contact and easy removal; the organiser said notice came after posting. A claimed corpus above 200,000 is the company’s figure, not a verified count of unauthorised sensitive sessions.

The original GDATF warning page is unavailable (410), but a contemporaneous 27 March 2026 Zoom Community post by GDATF survives and directly preserves the organiser's account of the false-identity registration, secret recording and subsequent removal from WebinarTV. vigil_assessment.factual_basis: 404 Media directly examined a posted educators’ meeting, its AI podcast derivative, and later anonymous recovery and health-support recordings with visible identities. Kimberly Dorris of the Graves’ Disease & Thyroid Foundation said her meeting used registration screening and a waiting room, was not intended to be recorded, and appeared on WebinarTV; her original public warning now returns 410, so that proposition is reported through 404 Media rather than independently retrieved from the original post. The teacher’s meeting was removed after request; removal of other content and copies is not established. WebinarTV CEO Michael Robertson told reporters he seeks host permission and views webinars as public; the reported specific cases place posting before contact and participants’ expectations at odds with that claim. Zoom reportedly found access by public links and external screen-recording tools, not a Zoom platform breach. The American Library Association posted an institutional removal warning. NBC’s indexed investigation offers independent context but the page returned 403. The site’s greater-than-200,000 number is a self-reported corpus, not a verified harm count.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: Three distinct boundaries operated: a reachable link was treated as permission to enter and record; the capture of individual participants was treated as authorised by a session’s discoverability or a purported host contact; and meeting material was repurposed into public archives and AI podcasts. The last use is materially different even if attendance itself had been valid. Technical uncertainty about the exact recording tool does not undo the observed governance path.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: The later sensitive-session reporting shows why “webinar” and a discoverable link are poor proxies for consent. The same content crossed entry, participant-capture and publication/derivative-purpose boundaries; each needs separate authority. Actual exposed names and faces in recovery and health contexts support a more serious realised privacy outcome than the site’s self-reported corpus number.
